title: The rehatnamas
hook: codes of conduct linked to the Tenth Guru's time, written down by Sikhs after him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poets of Anandpur: tradition remembers a Guru who gathered writers around him. Your line was a court of poets. Which poem did you read aloud? Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

A family keeps a list on the fridge. Shoes off at the door. Nobody eats until everyone sits. Say thank you to whoever cooked. Nobody voted on it, exactly. It grew out of how the family wanted to live, and somebody finally wrote it down. Sikhs have something like that list, on a much larger scale. After the Tenth Guru, Sikhs wrote down codes of how a Sikh should live: what to do at dawn, how to treat a guest, what to give, what to avoid. Today's word is the name for those written codes.
screen: `A LIST ON THE FRIDGE.` → `HOW WE WANT TO LIVE, WRITTEN DOWN.` → `CODES OF HOW A SIKH SHOULD LIVE.`

segments.voice: The word is rehatnama. Rehat is the Sikh word for a way of living, a discipline kept day after day. Nama means a written piece, a letter or a record. Put together, a rehatnama is a written code for living. Tradition links these codes to the circle around Guru Gobind Singh. Some carry the names of Sikhs remembered as close to him; one is linked with Bhai Nand Lal, remembered as a poet of the Guru's court. Sikhs wrote them down after the Guru's time, and that matters for how they're read. They are not scripture. They sit beside the Guru Granth Sahib, not inside it. What do they hold? Mostly ordinary things, which is the point. Rise early. Remember the Name. Bathe and recite the morning prayers. Share what you earn. Keep the hair uncut. Treat the Guru's word with honor. Look at a rehatnama and you see that faith, for the Sikhs who wrote them, was not only an inner feeling. It was a shape for the whole day. Here's the honest part. The rehatnamas don't all say the same thing. They differ in detail, and some contain lines that later Sikhs questioned or set aside. Scholars and Sikh bodies have read them carefully side by side. Out of that long conversation came a shared code that we'll meet later in the path, the Sikh Rehat Maryada. So a rehatnama is a window, not a final word: a look at how early Sikhs tried to put the Gurus' teaching into daily practice, written down by people who cared enough to try.
screen: `REHAT, A WAY OF LIVING. NAMA, A WRITING.` · `WRITTEN DOWN AFTER THE GURU'S TIME.` · `A SHAPE FOR THE WHOLE DAY.` · `THEY DIFFER; A SHARED CODE CAME LATER.` · then, large: `A CODE FOR LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line of your own code. Settle, and breathe. Think about how you actually want your days to go, not how you think you ought to want them. Then find one plain line. Phone down at the table. Answer kindly before answering fast. Give something away each week. Make it short enough to fit on a fridge. If you have paper, write it. If not, say it once in your head. Then sit with it until the bell, and notice whether it still fits. The bell holds the time.
Rehatnama. A written code of Sikh living, linked by tradition to the Tenth Guru's circle and written down after him. Today's word.
Your line: a code for living. Today, keep the one line you wrote, once, on purpose, and see what it costs you. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Sikh historians and teachers read the rehatnamas as early records of Sikh discipline; for daily practice, gurdwaras and Sikh families follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a shared code drawn up later.
